course.name: King's Indian Defence
course.intro: Your Black repertoire against 1.d4 and everything else: the same set-up (...Nf6, ...g6, ...Bg7, ...O-O, ...d6) and two pawn breaks, ...e5 and ...c5. Most of your opponents never play the main-line King’s Indian, so the course starts with the systems you actually meet.

principles.title: Let White take the centre, then hit it
principles.short: The King’s Indian lets White build a big pawn centre and then attacks it with pawns.
principles.body: You don’t fight for the centre with your first moves: ...Nf6, ...g6, ...Bg7 and ...O-O get your king safe and your best bishop aiming at d4. The fight starts a few moves later, when a pawn break (...e5 or ...c5) hits White’s centre. If you never strike, White simply has more space for free.

principles.title: Pawn breaks are your counterplay
principles.short: Your play comes from ...e5 or ...c5 (and later ...f5). Prepare one and play it.
principles.body: Around moves 6 to 10, pick a break: ...e5 (usually prepared with ...Nbd7 or ...Nc6, or ...Re8) or ...c5 (hitting d4 from the side). Before you push, count: how many White pieces hit the square, and how many of yours defend it? In your games, many first mistakes were slower moves played when a break was available.

principles.title: The g7 bishop is your best piece
principles.short: Keep the long diagonal open and don’t swap the g7 bishop cheaply.
principles.body: The bishop on g7 guards your king and x-rays d4, c3 and b2. Opening the centre with ...e5xd4 or ...c5xd4 makes it stronger. White often tries to trade it with Qd2 and Bh6. When you can, answer by striking the centre (...e5, ...c5) so the trade costs White time, and keep the h-file closed.

principles.title: Leave your king’s pawn shield alone
principles.short: Moves like ...h6, ...Kh7, ...h5 or ...g5 loosen your king. Only play them with a concrete reason.
principles.body: After ...O-O your king is protected by the f7, g6 and h7 pawns and the g7 bishop. Every pawn move there creates a hole White can use (h6 for a bishop, g6 as a target for h4-h5). In your games, ...h6 and ...Kh7 were among the most common first mistakes: they spend a move without hitting the centre. Exceptions: ...h5 to stop h4-h5, and ...f5 when the centre is closed.

principles.title: Develop, castle, then fight
principles.short: Knights and bishops out, king castled, then the pawn break. Don’t move a piece twice or bring the queen out early.
principles.body: The KID set-up is fast: ...Nf6, ...g6, ...Bg7, ...O-O, ...d6. Then the queen’s knight (to d7 or c6) supports the break. Moving the queen early or a piece twice gives White time to grab space.

principles.title: Don’t let e4-e5 kick your knight
principles.short: When White can play e4 and e5, put a pawn on d6 first so e5 can be met by ...dxe5.
principles.body: Your f6 knight is your main defender. If White gets a pawn to e5 while it can’t be captured, the knight has to run and White gains time and space. That’s why ...d6 comes before ...Bg7 or ...O-O when White already has Nc3 and e4. If e5 does come, a quick ...Nh5 (hitting a bishop on f4) or ...Nfd7 hits back.

principles.title: Checks, captures, threats: both ways
principles.short: Before every move: what did White’s last move allow, and what does my move leave undefended?
principles.body: Look at White’s last move first. Did it leave a pawn or piece loose (a free pawn on e4 or b2)? Does it threaten something (Nd5 hitting c7, e4-e5 forking)? Then blunder-check your own move. Across your games, about a third of the first mistakes were missed captures, and you cashed in only about 6 in 10 of your opponents’ blunders.

principles.title: Hunt White’s active bishop
principles.short: ...Nh5 against a bishop on f4 or g5, ...Ng4 against a bishop on e3: winning the bishop pair is worth a move.
principles.body: In the London and Jobava, White’s dark-squared bishop on f4 is its best piece and it fights your g7 bishop. ...Nh5 attacks it: if it retreats, you have gained time; if White allows ...Nxf4 or ...Nxg3, you have the bishop pair and your g7 bishop has no rival.

principles.title: Closed centre: attack where your pawns point
principles.short: When White plays d5, your d6-e5 pawns point at the kingside: play ...Nd7/...Ne8/...Nh5, ...f5, ...f4, ...g5.
principles.body: Once White locks the centre with d4-d5, the game splits into two races. White attacks on the queenside (c5, b4), and you attack the king with ...f5-f4 and ...g5-g4. The knight on f6 has to move first to let the f-pawn go: ...Nd7, ...Ne8 or ...Nh5.

principles.title: Open centre: pieces and files
principles.short: After pawn trades in the centre (dxe5 dxe5, ...cxd4), use open files, the d4 square and the long diagonal.
principles.body: When the centre opens, the game is about piece activity: rooks to open files (...Re8, ...Rd8), knights to central squares (d4 is a classic outpost), and the g7 bishop on the open long diagonal. In queenless positions after dxe5 dxe5 Qxd8, watch for Nd5 hitting c7 and e7.

principles.title: Against quiet systems, strike before you’re squeezed
principles.short: The London, Colle and e3 set-ups give you time. Use it for a break by move 8-10, not for waiting moves.
principles.body: Quiet systems don’t attack you early, so the danger is drifting: ...b6, ...a6, ...h6, ...Qd7 and similar moves let White finish developing and gain space. Against the London, ...c5 and ...Qb6 hit d4 and b2 (the bishop has left c1, so b2 is often weak). Against the Colle, ...e5 is easy because no White bishop watches e5.

principles.title: When White attacks your king, hit back in the centre
principles.short: Against Qd2, Bh6, h4 and O-O-O: answer h4 with ...h5, and counter with ...c5, ...e5 or ...b5.
principles.body: White’s fastest attack against the KID is Qd2, Bh6 (to trade your bishop) and h4-h5 (to open the h-file). Don’t wait for it: a central break opens lines against a king that has castled long, and ...h5 stops h4-h5 in its tracks.

plan.structure: White: d4, e3, c3 with bishops on f4 and d3 (or e2). You: g6-d6, then ...c5.
ideas: Hit d4 with ...c5. After ...cxd4 exd4 the e-file is half-open: ...Re8 and ...e5 follow.
...Qb6 eyes b2: the bishop has left c1, so b2 is often defended only by the queen.
...Nh5 chases the f4 bishop. Winning the bishop pair leaves your g7 bishop without a rival.
Don’t drift: ...h6, ...a6 and ...b6 let White finish developing and squeeze you.
plan.yourGames: Your most common London. Your first mistake came at a median of move 12, often around ...Bg4 and the h3 question, or after a slow kingside pawn move.

chapters.name: Colle and e3 systems
chapters.white: 1.d4, Nf3, e3 and Bd3, without Bf4

plan.structure: White: d4-e3 (often c3 or b3), bishop on d3 or e2. You: g6-d6, then ...e5.
ideas: No White bishop watches e5, so ...e5 is easy: prepare it with ...Nbd7 or ...Nc6.
If White pushes e3-e4, the centre often opens: take on d4 when it helps your pieces and use the e-file.
Against b3 and Bb2, ...e5 also blocks the long diagonal toward your king.
Don’t drift: you scored only 37% against these set-ups, often after slow moves like ...b6, ...h6 or ...Qd7.
plan.yourGames: Your lowest-scoring group of systems (37%). The first mistakes came early (a median of move 9 against 1.e3 set-ups).

chapters.name: Jobava, Barry and e4 attacks
chapters.white: 1.d4 with Nc3 and Bf4, Be3 or Qd2, often e4

plan.structure: White: Nc3 and a quick e4, often with Qd2, Bh6 and long castling. You: ...d6 in time, then ...c5, ...e5 or ...c6 and ...b5.
ideas: Put ...d6 in before White can play e4-e5 to kick your f6 knight.
If e4-e5 does come with a bishop on f4, ...Nh5! hits the bishop and the e5 pawn often falls.
Against Qd2 and Bh6, strike in the centre with ...e5 or ...c5. Against h4, answer ...h5.
Careful with queen trades: after dxe5 dxe5 Qxd8, Nd5 hits c7. You lost twice to Nd5 and Nxc7 mate in this line.
plan.yourGames: The earliest mistakes of any system: 57% of these games had a mistake by move 10 (median move 9).

plan.structure: White: the big centre with c4, d4 and e4. You: ...d6 and ...e5. When White plays d5, the centre locks.
ideas: Meet the big centre with ...e5 (or ...c5 against f3, f4 or Bg5 set-ups).
If White plays d5, attack on the kingside: the knight moves (…Ne8, …Nd7, …Nh5), then ...f5, ...f4, ...g5.
If White trades with dxe5 dxe5 Qxd8, the d4 square and the d-file matter. Watch Nd5 and Bg5 tricks.
White attacks on the queenside (b4, c5). Your attack has to be faster.
plan.yourGames: You meet the true main lines only now and then (27 games, mostly the Classical with Nf3 and Be2).

chapters.name: Quiet c4 systems and the Fianchetto

plan.structure: White: c4 and d4 with e3, Bf4, Bg5 or g3. You: the KID set-up, then ...e5 or ...c5.
ideas: Against e3, play ...Nbd7 and ...e5: White has less space than in the main lines.
Against Bf4 or Bg5, ...c5 hits d4; after exd4, ...Qb6 eyes b2.
Against the Fianchetto (g3, Bg2), ...Nbd7 and ...e5 with ...c6 and ...Re8.
plan.yourGames: 34 games with c4 but no e4, where you scored 60%, plus 5 Fianchetto games where you scored 20%.

plan.structure: White: an early Bg5, often Bxf6. You: the bishop pair and the long diagonal.
ideas: If White takes on f6, you get the bishop pair. Open the position for it.
After Bxf6 Bxf6, b2 is often loose on the long diagonal: check ...Bxb2 every move.
Against the Torre with Nbd2 and c3: ...Nbd7 and ...e5.
plan.yourGames: 14 games, but 67% of the Torre games had a mistake by move 10, including a missed free pawn on b2.

plan.structure: White: a fianchetto or a quiet set-up. You: the same KID set-up, then ...e5.
ideas: The set-up is the same against almost everything: ...Nf6, ...g6, ...Bg7, ...O-O, ...d6, ...e5.
Against a fianchetto, ...e5 and ...Nc6 build a solid centre; ...a5 stops b4.
Against 1.b3 and Bb2, ...e5 blocks the long diagonal toward your king.
plan.yourGames: You scored well here: 69% against 1.Nf3 and 71% against 1.c4.

chapters.name: Early tricks: take the free pawn

plan.structure: White offers a pawn on move 2. You: take it, then develop normally.
ideas: Before playing your set-up move, look at what White’s last move allows: 2.e4?! leaves the pawn hanging.
After ...Nxe4, bring the knight back to f6 when it is attacked, then develop as usual.
plan.yourGames: In three games you answered 2.e4?! with 2...g6 or 2...d6 instead of taking: Stockfish rates 2...Nxe4 more than half a pawn better.

plan.q: You have just played ...e5. If White trades with dxe5 dxe5, what should you aim for?
options: Active pieces in the open centre: rooks on the d- and e-files, a knight heading for d4, the g7 bishop on an open diagonal
Push ...h6 and ...g5 to attack the bishop
Trade queens and offer a draw
plan.why: Open centre: pieces and files. After the pawn trade your pieces are as active as White’s, and the d4 square is a natural home for a knight.

plan.q: This position also arises after 6.O-O c5 7.c3. What does that tell you?
options: One plan (...c5, ...Nc6, ...cxd4, ...Re8, ...e5) covers most London move orders
You need a different set-up for every White move order
plan.why: Learning plans instead of move lists: the same structure keeps coming back, so the same ideas work.

plan.q: Your knight on h5 attacks the bishop on g3. What is the point?
options: Win the bishop pair with ...Nxg3, so your g7 bishop has no rival on the dark squares
plan.why: Hunt White’s active bishop. Trading your knight for the London bishop leaves your g7 bishop as the strongest minor piece on the board.

plan.q: Why does ...Qb6 work so well against the London?
options: The bishop left c1, so b2 has few defenders, and the queen also hits d4
plan.why: Against quiet systems, find the targets: in the London they are d4 and b2.

plan.q: After ...Nh5, what is your idea?
plan.why: Hunt the active bishop. Black is already slightly better (Stockfish about +0.3).

plan.q: After 8.dxe5 dxe5, where does your d7 knight want to go?
options: c5, hitting the d3 bishop and the e4 pawn
plan.why: Open centre: pieces and squares. ...Nc5 is a classic King’s Indian route once the d-file has opened.

plan.q: White has pawns on d4 and e4. What does ...c5 do?
options: Attacks d4 again; if White pushes d5 your knight gets the e5 square
Prepares ...b5 and a queenside pawn storm
Nothing: it is a waiting move
plan.why: Pawn breaks are your counterplay. Every break in this line targets White’s d4 pawn.

plan.q: Why did you play ...e5 against the b2 bishop?
options: To blunt the bishop’s long diagonal toward g7 and your king, and to hit d4
To win a pawn by force
plan.why: The g7 and b2 bishops face each other; a pawn on e5 shields your side of the diagonal.

plan.q: White’s pawn is on e3, not e4. What does that mean after ...e5?
options: White has less space, so your pieces have more room. You can also play ...e4 later to gain space
plan.why: Against quiet systems, take your share of the centre with the break.

plan.q: With pawns on d4, e3 and f4, which square has White weakened?
options: e4: no White pawn can control it any more
plan.why: Every pawn move leaves squares behind. Your pieces can aim at e4 (...Bf5, ...Ne4 later).

lines.name: 4.e4 d6 5.e5: ...Nh5! and the e5 pawn falls

plan.q: Why does ...dxe5 work after 6.Be3 but not straight after 5.e5?
options: With ...Nh5 played first, the bishop has been driven off f4, so e5 can be won without Nd5 tricks against c7
plan.why: Checks, captures, threats: the order of moves decides whether a capture wins a pawn or walks into a trap.

plan.q: What principle won you the e5 pawn in this line?
options: Hunt the active bishop: ...Nh5 drove away e5’s defender, so the pawn fell
plan.why: Hunt White’s active bishop: the f4 bishop was the only piece holding e5.

plan.q: White has castled long with the queen on h6. What is your plan?
options: Counterattack: ...b5 or ...Qa5 on the queenside, plus pressure on d4 and e4
plan.why: When White attacks your king, hit back in the centre and toward White’s king.

plan.q: Why is ...c5 strong when White’s knight is on c3?
options: White can’t answer with c3, so d4 is harder to defend
plan.why: Find the target: the knight on c3 blocks the c-pawn that would normally defend d4.

plan.q: This is the third line where you play ...c5, ...cxd4 and ...Nc6. Why does it keep working?
options: White’s set-up leaves d4 short of pawn support, and the g7 bishop adds pressure on it
It only works against strong players
plan.why: One plan, many move orders: d4 is the target.

plan.q: Why ...d6 on move 3 instead of ...Bg7?
options: So that e4-e5 can be answered by ...dxe5 instead of moving the f6 knight again
plan.why: Don’t let e4-e5 kick your knight.

plan.q: Which break are you preparing with ...c6 and ...Nbd7?
plan.why: Pawn breaks are your counterplay: ...Nbd7 supports ...e5.

plan.q: White has pawns on d4, e4 and f4. How do you fight them?
plan.why: Let White take the centre, then hit it.

plan.q: The centre is locked. Where do you attack?
options: The kingside with ...g5-g4, toward White’s king (where your pawns point)
plan.why: Closed centre: attack where your pawns point. Your d6-e5-f4 chain points at White’s kingside.

plan.q: White is pushing on the queenside with b4. What is your answer?
options: Race on the kingside with ...f5, ...f4 and ...g5
plan.why: Closed centre: attack where your pawns point, and make your attack faster than White’s.

plan.q: With queens off, what decides this kind of position?
options: Piece activity and key squares such as d4 and d5
A direct attack on the king
Who has more pawns on the kingside
plan.why: Open centre: pieces and files.

plan.q: Why ...a5 here?
options: To stop White’s b4 and secure c5 for your knight
plan.why: In closed centres, slow your opponent’s pawn storm and give your pieces good squares.

plan.q: What was the idea of ...Ng4?
options: Hunt White’s dark-squared bishop and gain time
plan.why: Hunt White’s active bishop.

plan.q: Why ...f5 now?
options: It hits e4, the base of White’s centre, while the bishop is back on c1
plan.why: Pawn breaks are your counterplay: ...f5 is the King’s Indian’s third break.

plan.q: White has castled long. Which of your breaks is most useful?
plan.why: When White attacks, hit back in the centre and toward White’s king.

plan.q: What is the problem with White’s four centre pawns?
options: They are hard to support, and every pawn break opens lines for your pieces
plan.why: Let White take the centre, then hit it.

plan.q: Why ...c5 instead of ...e5 here?
options: The g5 bishop pins the knight and makes ...e5 hard; ...c5 hits d4 instead
plan.why: Two breaks: if one is hard to play, use the other.

plan.q: What will you do if White plays d5 after ...e5?
options: Plan ...Nc5 and ...a5, then ...f5 after the f6 knight moves
Play ...c6 and open the queenside at any cost
plan.why: Closed centre: good squares for your knights, then the kingside break.

plan.q: Why ...Re8?
options: It supports e5 and prepares for the e-file to open
It protects the king from Bd3
plan.why: Develop with purpose: the rook belongs on the file that will open.

plan.q: Which White pawn is your main target here?
plan.why: Find the target: d4 is hit by your knight, bishop and the c-file.

plan.q: Your queen on b6 hits two targets. Which?
plan.why: With White’s dark-squared bishop away from c1, b2 is loose.

plan.q: After ...exd4 Nxd4, what is your target?
options: The e4 pawn, hit by the rook, queen and f6 knight
plan.why: Open centre: pieces and files. The half-open e-file points at e4.

plan.q: You have two bishops against bishop and knight. What do they want?
options: Open lines: pawn breaks like ...c5 and ...f4
plan.why: The bishop pair is strongest in open positions.

plan.q: Why ...Qe8?
options: To break the pin on the f6 knight
plan.why: A pinned knight can’t join the fight. Unpin, then play.

plan.q: After Bxf6 Bxf6, what should you check every move?
options: Whether b2 or d4 is loose on the long diagonal
Whether your rook can reach h8
plan.why: Checks, captures, threats: in your games you missed a free pawn on b2 in this exact structure.

lines.name: King's Indian Attack: 1.Nf3, g3, d3, e4

plan.q: The position is nearly symmetrical. What will decide it?
options: Who gets their pawn break in first (...f5 for you, f4 for White)
plan.why: Pawn breaks are your counterplay.

plan.q: Why ...a5?
options: To slow White’s b4 and queenside expansion
To open the a-file for your rook
plan.why: Restrain your opponent’s plan before carrying out yours.

lines.name: English with e4 and d4: a transposition

plan.q: You are in the Classical King’s Indian. What is your plan if White plays d5?
plan.why: Closed centre: attack where your pawns point.

plan.q: After 7.fxe5, how do you get the pawn back?
plan.why: Checks, captures, threats: count the attackers on e5.

plan.q: Which plan from the Colle chapter did you use here?
plan.why: One plan, many move orders.

plan.q: What habit would have saved this pawn in your games?
options: Asking “what did White’s last move allow?” before playing my set-up move
plan.why: Checks, captures, threats: both ways, every move.

plan.q: White attacked your e4 knight with d3. What is the safest retreat?
plan.why: Develop and consolidate when you are ahead in material.

Nf6.t: A knight toward the centre that stops e2-e4 for now. The King's Indian starts like this against almost everything.

Bf4.t: The London System: the bishop comes out before e3 shuts it in.

Nc3.t: The Jobava London (Nc3 and Bf4) or the Barry Attack.

c4.t: The main line: White takes space on the queenside.

Bg5.t: The Trompowsky: White offers to give up the bishop for your knight.

e4.t: A gambit: the e4 pawn is unprotected.

g6.t: Preparing ...Bg7. You let White keep the centre for now and aim a bishop at it.

Nf3.t: White's usual plan: Nf3, e3, Bd3 or Be2, castle, then c3 and h3.

Bg7.t: On the long diagonal the bishop guards your king and x-rays d4 and b2.

e3.t: Supports d4 and lets the light-squared bishop out.

d6.t: Takes control of e5 and prepares both breaks, ...e5 and ...c5. Castling first is just as good.

Bd3.t: Club players usually put the bishop here, aiming at h7 behind your g6 pawn.

Be2.t: A modest square, the masters' choice. The bishop doesn't aim at h7, but it can't be hit by ...e5-e4 either.

O-O.t: King safe, rook connected. Now the fight for the centre can start.

c3.t: A different move order: c3 before castling.

Nbd2.t: The knight supports e4. It doesn't cover d4, so ...c5 is even stronger.

c5.t: Hit d4 from the side. This is the main plan against the London: attack the base of White's centre before White is fully set up.

Bg4.t: Playable, but after h3 you have to choose between giving up the bishop pair with ...Bxf3 or retreating. In your games this bishop often ended up passive on d7. ...c5 keeps the initiative.

h6.t: A waiting move. It loosens g6 and does nothing for the centre.

c3.t: Supports d4, so ...cxd4 can be met by exd4 or cxd4.

dxc5.t: White takes the pawn, but it can't be kept.

Nc6.t: The knight joins the pressure on d4.

h3.t: Stops ...Bg4 and gives the f4 bishop a retreat on h2.

cxd4.t: Opening the c-file and, after exd4, the e-file. Your g7 bishop's diagonal gets longer.

exd4.t: Recapturing toward the centre. Now the e-file matters.

Re8.t: The rook stands on the half-open e-file and supports ...e5.

Qb6.t: Also good, hitting b2 and d4. ...Re8 is simpler because it prepares the break.

e5.t: The break arrives. Your pieces are active and the game is equal: exactly what you want from the opening.

c5.t: Same plan: hit d4. Move orders change, your plan doesn't.

Nc6.t: Fine too, but ...c5 keeps the c-pawn free and works against every London set-up.

c5.t: Hit d4 before White gets c3 and e4 in.

e5.t: With the e-file open, the ...e5 break comes at once and asks the f4 bishop where it's going.

Bg3.t: The bishop steps back and keeps an eye on e5.

Nh5.t: Now the bishop is hunted on g3: ...Nxg3 would win the bishop pair.

dxe5.t: The centre opens and Black is slightly better (Stockfish about +0.3).

h3.t: The most common master move: a retreat square for the bishop on h2 and no ...Bg4.

c5.t: The main reply in master games: hit d4.

cxd4.t: Trade first, so the queen can come to b6 with pressure on d4 and b2.

Nc6.t: Natural, but Stockfish prefers trading on d4 first, so that ...Qb6 hits two targets.

Qb6.t: The queen hits b2 and d4. With the bishop gone from c1, only White's queen defends b2.

Qb3.t: Offering a queen trade to cover b2.

Nc6.t: Develop and keep the tension. If Qxb6 axb6, your rook gets the half-open a-file.

dxc5.t: Recapture. The d-file opens and your queen faces White's.

Nh5.t: The f4 bishop is the target. ...Nxf4 next would give you the bishop pair and the dark squares.

g6.t: The same set-up as against the London.

e3.t: The Colle: a quiet pawn on e3 and the bishop to d3.

O-O.t: Castle quickly. Nothing is happening yet.

c3.t: The classic Colle: c3, Nbd2 and e4.

b3.t: The Colle-Zukertort: the bishop goes to b2, aiming down the long diagonal.

Nbd7.t: The knight supports ...e5. On d7 it also keeps the c-pawn free.

h6.t: This kind of waiting move led to many of your problems in Colle games. Prepare ...e5 instead.

b6.t: Slow. The bishop on b7 bites on d5 and e4 while White grabs the centre.

e5.t: The classic King's Indian answer: meet e4 with ...e5.

dxe5.t: The centre is symmetrical and level. Your knight can reach c5, attacking the d3 bishop and e4.

Re8.t: The rook supports e5 and the knight on d7 can now move.

e5.t: Strike first, before White plays e4.

exd4.t: Release the tension so your rooks and the g7 bishop get open lines.

c5.t: Now hit the new d4 pawn. If d5, the knight comes to e5 and your pieces are very active.

Nc6.t: The knight supports ...e5 and pressures d4.

e5.t: Block the b2 bishop's diagonal and hit d4.

Nd7.t: Not ...dxe5?, which leaves your knight on c6 loose to tactics on the d-file and long diagonal. The knight on d7 regains the pawn.

Nxe5.t: Pawn regained, the long diagonal reopened for your bishop, and the game is level.

Bd3.t: Heading for the Stonewall with f4.

c4.t: White grabs some space on the queenside.

Nbd7.t: Prepares ...e5 and keeps the c-pawn free.

e5.t: The break. Against a pawn on e3 (not e4), ...e5 gives Black an easy game.

f4.t: The Stonewall: control of e5 and a kingside attack later.

c5.t: White's pawns on d4 and f4 leave e4 and the queenside soft. Hit d4.

e4.t: White builds the centre and threatens e5.
White grabs the centre at once.

e3.t: A London with Nc3 instead of c3.

d6.t: Now e4-e5 can be met by capturing on e5, or by ...Nh5.

e5.t: Kicking the knight. This is the critical moment.

Qd2.t: The attacking set-up: Bh6 to trade your bishop, long castling, then h4-h5.
